title: Knower of every heart
hook: ghat ghat ke antar kee jaanat: He knows every heart and recognizes the pain of good and bad alike (Chaupai)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one who spreads and gathers, and your line, spread and gathered. Did the doorways remind you? Today, a line about being known, all the way down. Day three hundred seventy-six.

There's a particular loneliness in being misunderstood. You did something for a good reason, and someone took it the worst way. Or you're carrying a pain nobody can see, so people treat you as if you're fine. Or, harder, you did something wrong, and you know it, and nobody can see the mess of reasons and hurt underneath. Plenty of people walk around partly hidden, even from the people who love us. Sometimes, especially from them. Chaupai has a line for exactly that hiddenness, and it goes further than you'd expect. Today: knower of every heart.
screen: `THE LONELINESS OF BEING MISUNDERSTOOD.` → `PAIN NOBODY CAN SEE.` → `PARTLY HIDDEN, EVEN FROM LOVED ONES.`

segments.voice: The line, transliterated, is ghat ghat ke antar kee jaanat, bhale bure kee peer pachhaanat. Ghat ghat: every vessel, every body, every heart. Ke antar kee jaanat: knows what's inside. Bhale bure: the good and the bad. Kee peer pachhaanat: recognizes the pain of. He knows what's within every heart, and recognizes the pain of the good and the bad alike. The first half is something Sikh scripture says often. God is antarjami, the inner knower, the one who sees from inside. But the second half is the surprise. The pain of the bad. Not just the good person's suffering. The wrongdoer's too. Follow that through. The person who hurt you has a pain underneath it, and in this line, God recognizes that as well. It doesn't excuse anything. The same prayer has just asked for wrongdoers to be stopped. But it refuses to pretend that anyone, good or bad, is only their actions. Peer, the word for pain here, is close to an ordinary Punjabi word for an ache, the kind you'd mention to a doctor. That's how close this knowing is. And here's the other side of it. If the One knows every heart, then you are known, completely. Your good reasons that nobody saw. Your hidden ache. Even the tangle behind the thing you're ashamed of. For some people that sounds frightening. Chaupai sets it inside a prayer for protection, so it's meant to sound like rest. In the prayer's picture, the one praying has nothing to explain. They're already understood.
screen: `GHAT GHAT: EVERY HEART.` · `ANTARJAMI: THE INNER KNOWER.` · `THE PAIN OF THE BAD, TOO.` · `BEING KNOWN, MEANT AS REST.` · then, large: `HE KNOWS THE PAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be known, and rest. Sit and breathe slowly. Bring to mind something about yourself that nobody fully understands. An old hurt. A reason you've never said out loud. A worry you carry quietly. You don't need to fix it or explain it. Just let it be there, in the open. Then picture it already seen, completely, by someone who isn't shocked. If you pray, you can say Waheguru and let the One who knows every heart hold it. If you don't, just practice not hiding it from yourself. The bell holds the time.
Knower of every heart. Ghat ghat ke antar kee jaanat: the One knows what's inside every heart, and recognizes the pain of the good and the bad alike.
Your line: he knows the pain. Today, when someone acts badly, wonder for one second about the pain underneath, without excusing it. Day three hundred seventy-six.

screen: `DAY 376 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SINCE I HELD YOUR FEET.`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this line within Chaupai Sahib morning and evening, and Sikh scripture often names God as antarjami, the inner knower of every heart.

fork.setup: someone has hurt you badly. Chaupai says the One knows every heart. whose pain does the line say God recognizes?
options: the pain of the good and the bad alike.
fork.reveal: bhale bure kee peer pachhaanat: the pain of the good and the bad. it doesn't excuse the harm, but it sees what's underneath.

original.script: ਘਟ ਘਟ ਕੇ ਅੰਤਰ ਕੀ ਜਾਨਤ
original.say: GHUT GHUT kay UN-tar kee JAA-nat
original.note: Gurmukhi: knows what is within every heart, the first half of Chaupai's line.

trapdoor: what you thought: God knows everything you do wrong.
what it means: the One knows every heart and recognizes the pain of the good and the bad alike. being known is meant as rest.
what a scholar hears: ghat, a pot or vessel, is the scriptures' common image for the body; peer, pain, sits in the line beside bhale bure, so compassion reaches even the wrongdoer.

sources.ref: Benti Chaupai (Chaupai Sahib), verse 'ghat ghat ke antar kee jaanat'

notes: Transliteration 'ghat ghat ke antar kee jaanat, bhale bure kee peer pachhaanat'; confirm spelling and the reading that the pain recognized is of both good and bad.
Peer linked to the everyday Punjabi word for an ache (peerh): confirm.
Ghat as pot/vessel for the body: confirm.
Antarjami as a frequent name in Sikh scripture: Keeper may add an Ang.
